items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I move, That the House take
note of miscellaneous business . Within the last 24 hours we have learnt of outrageous
activity relating to the police investigation of  the so-called teacup tape, recorded during
the election campaign 2011. A cameraman left a tape recorder on a cafe table where
John Key and John Banks sat. It was a media stunt, of course, in trying to organise a
coalition Government. To prevent publica tion of the tape’s contents, John Key
complained to the police. The police were under pressure to complete the investigation,
and we understand that the Prime Minister’s ch ief of staff was kept “in the loop” during
the investigation.
New Zealand First has learnt that the pol ice recorded discussions to seize the
telephone records of a private citizen so that they could lay charges against the
cameraman. That citizen was me. That is ri ght—my telephone records were going to be
seized in an operation that was sparked by the Prime Minister’s office and monitored by
the Prime Minister’s office.
This is not Zimbabwe; this is New Zeala nd. If there had been a security issue at
stake, I would have handed over my cellpho ne records and any other records to the
authorities immediately, but there was not.
There is information in a police file that says that police would have taken my phone
records to lay charges and make a case ag ainst Bradley Ambrose. If Mr Eagleson, Mr
Key’s chief of staff, was bei ng kept “in the loop” during th e investigation, it stands to
reason that the boss, John Key, would also ha ve been in the loop as well. That is
perhaps the reason he backed off demanding a prosecution: he would have had to admit
that his politically motivated use of the pol ice led to a private citizen’s phone records
being accessed illegally. And it is the reas on why today, when asked that critical
question, he refused to answer without advice.
I was nowhere near the cafe. I have far better things to do.
There is another element to this gross inva sion of privacy—a rather sinister element.
Why would a group of people in the Prime Mi nister’s office, funded by the taxpayers,
be involved in a police inves tigation during an election camp aign? This was not a leak
from a State intelligence agency. This was not  a matter of national security, or even a
matter of life and death; it was about a petula nt Prime Minister tryi ng to save his face
and his backside.

items.speaker: Now we have to ask
items.text: did he actually sign a warrant, or was he prepared to? Did the
police look at my phone records anyway? How did they know that they had to seize
them to carry out a successful prosecution ? Why did the police zero in on me, for
example?
After the recorder was found, a voice on th e tape broadcast on YouTube pointed out
that a guy in a New Zealand First T-shirt was present outside the cafe. That meant that
12444 General Debate 7 Aug 2013
New Zealand First was suspected at the outse t, despite the fact that people wearing T-
shirts with “New Zealand First” on them are legion all over the country, in their tens of
thousands.
At the time I was a private citizen. This information is contained in briefing notes
handed from the Wellington police to the Auckland police. The officer told his
counterpart that whatever they  decided to do, they were to  brief Mr Eagleson. This is
not Zimbabwe. Today I am asking the Prime Mi nister and the police to come clean and
produce all the documents relating to my reco rds and the teacup tape investigation. As
we have found out, the Prime Minister’s office was donkey deep in violations of
privacy, and guess what? The same Wayne Ea gleson has his fingerp rints and the Prime
Minister’s DNA over all the files.
In my years in this House, under eight Pr ime Ministers, I have never experienced
such a personal outrage and an absolute a buse of power by the executive. It had nothing
to do with anything other than an election stunt. This was a humble, private citizen. This
is corruption that goes to the core of this country’s activities under this Prime Minister,
and every member of this House should be  joining New Zealand First in condemning
this in the strongest possible terms.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: The contamination of
whey protein concentrate is an issue that  has been the key focus of mine and the
Government’s over the last 6 or so days. Si nce it was notified on Friday, no other issue
has been a priority for this  Government. There is a wide  range of Ministers who are
involved, working across their respective areas . Right now the focus is squarely on the
health and well-being of our children and fa milies, both here in New Zealand and, of
course, in those overseas mark ets. The Ministry for Primar y Industries is continuing to
work around the clock, seeking to clarify with certainty the extent of the potential
contamination. Earlier this week the Minist ry for Primary Industries sent staff into
Fonterra’s data and distribution centres and Nutricia ware houses, with their permission,
to verify the information and gain a complete  picture. Ministry of Health officials are
working with a range of organisations such  as Plunket and Heath line, and, of course,
information is regularly available on the Mi nistry for Primary Industries’ website. We
want to ensure that the information is getting out there to the people who need it most.
Of course, everyone in this House will be  aware that Nutric ia has initiated a
voluntary recall of Nutricia Karicare Stage 1 New Baby Infant Formula, for babies from
birth, and Nutricia Karicare  Gold+ Stage 2 Follow-on Form ula, for babies from 6
months onwards. I acknowledge my ministerial colleagues Mi nister Ryall, Minister
Goodhew, and, indeed, Minister  Kaye as well, who are in volved in doing a very good
response in this area, working very closel y across these Government departments to
ensure that this information is flowing through to consumers here and, indeed, in other
international markets. If parents or caregive rs have any of the recalled product lines at
home, they should return them to the shop that  they have been bought from, or return to
the place of purchase, and seek a refund.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade is working with its embassies to provide
information to international markets. This issue has the potential to affect children in
other countries, and we want to do what we can to ensure their overall safety. I
appreciate that information changed in the first few days, and that is now becoming a lot
clearer. Although the informati on has not been completely cl ear at times, officials and
the Government have been taking and will  continue to take a very conservative,
precautionary approach. I acknowledge Minist ers Groser and McCully for providing
that information through to those embassi es on a regular and timely time frame. I
understand that there are a lo t of questions, and right now our focus is on ensuring the
health and safety of consumers in New Zealand and across the world. I can assure
7 Aug 2013 General Debate 12445
everyone in the House and the New Zealand public that at the appropriate time I will
ask those questions, as will the Government, to  ensure that we get the answers that we
all require.
This incident also affects our international reputation. It will have an effect, but it is
hard to measure—very hard to quantify at th is stage. The fortnightly global trade online
auction last night was of some comfort to some exporters. There was a mild dip back by
about 2.4 percent in the auction prices. To me , this result indicates that the market has
taken a measured response on the current si tuation. There was strong interest from
around 200 bidders and a rise in  that, in the last aucti on, and although whole-milk
powder was back by 1.6 percen t and skim-milk powder was b ack by 3 percent, it was
very similar, when you weigh up that, ove rall, the online auction has been moving
around quite a bit.
As you know, Mr Speaker, and as the H ouse knows, there has been a lot of
disappointment about what has happened, but  New Zealand has a st rong history as an
exporting food nation for over 100 years. We need to maintain our integrity on the
world stage. Something has gone wrong. We need to rectify what has gone wrong and
maintain our integrity, and our integrity will be measured on how we respond. This is an
important issue and I want to conclude by saying that the Government is doing all it can
to provide information to New Zealand consumers and international markets.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Today I want to talk about
jobs, but before I do I want to say that the allegations that have been raised by Winston
Peters in the House today about the accessing of his cellphone records is an extremely
serious allegation. It sits alongside the be haviour that we have seen from this
Government and from John Key and his offi ce, in particular, that shows no respect
whatsoever for the privacy of New Zealand ci tizens. Be it a journalist in the form of
Andrea Vance, be it a politician, or be it the Government Communications Security
Bureau and all New Zealanders, the respect fo r the rule of law and privacy from this
Government is seriously in question today. The fact that the Prime Minister’s office
thinks that it can direct Parliamentary Serv ice adds to that. This Government does not
respect the privacy of New Zealand citizen s, and it does not respect the separation
between the executive and other parts of the parliamentary complex.
The Labour Party was formed on the basis th at the value and contribution of workers
to the economy need to be recognised. Our guiding beliefs are about the value of work:
a fair day’s pay for a fair day’s work. But,  more than that, Labour  recognises that in
work lie things that are of gr eat significance to New Zealande rs, to their self-esteem, to
their ability to provide for their families and care for their families, and to their
contribution to society. Work and jobs—good, sa fe jobs—are at the heart of Labour’s
vision for the society we want to live in. Jobs and work ar e at the heart of our policy,
which is why it gives Labour and me no comfort whatsoever to learn today that 153,000
New Zealanders are out of work—unemployed. We have no pleasure that in the last 3
months 5,000 jobs have been lost. These are not just statistics; these are real people with
families to look after and mortgages to pay who are losing their jobs.
From Dunedin to Dannevirke, from Nels on to Napier, jobs are being lost and
families’ lives are being put at risk. And th ese real stories range right across the age
groups, from the young graduate who came to  see me 8 months af ter graduating, who
after 100 applications for jobs but no job doe s not know what to do with his future, to
the gentleman from Christchurch whom I found sticking his CV under the door of my
electorate office, having also applied for n early 100 jobs since leaving Christchurch to
come to Wellington. Those jobs are not there for those people.
New Zealanders have given the National Party the benefit of the doubt—the global
financial crisis, the Christchurch ear thquakes—but now is the time when New
12446 General Debate 7 Aug 2013
Zealanders should be seeing some hope from this Government that things will get better
on the job front. Instead, all there is is fear that  they will lose their jobs. In actual fact, it
is the earthquake, or rather the recovery from the earthquake, that is now propping up
the job market. It is no longer possible for this Government to use the excuse of the
earthquake. The Government is meant to be helping with the recovery.
It is no longer right for this Government to continue to blame the global financial
crisis nearly 5 years after it took office. It promised  New Zealanders 170,000 new jobs.
It will fall woefully short of that mark. In the last 2 years only 17,000 jobs have been
created. That is across 2 whole years. That is simply not enough from this Government.
Imagine just how much worse it would be if 200,000 Kiwis had not  taken flight to
Australia. Unemployment would be well over 8 percent.
So what does a proper jobs policy look like? Well, from Labour, what it will mean is
giving exporters a fair go, ge tting research and developm ent going, making sure that
training of workers is a prio rity, giving Kiwi companies a proper go at Government
contracts, and real regional development po licies that focus on indus tries where there is
growth—in manufacturing, in informati on and communications technology—not the
National Party’s approach of the search for a silver bullet that simply cannot be found.
It is only with Labour that that change to a real jobs policy will happen.
I want to finish with an old saying, to try to give comfort to some people who are out
there looking for work. They say that a recession is when someone you know loses their
job, and a depression is when you lose your job. The recovery starts when John Key
loses his.

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: The events that have unfurled in respect
of potentially contaminated infant form ula over the last, I do not know, 72 hours now
pose some very, very significant challenges for New Zealand, pose significant
challenges for the Government, both at the political level and the official level, and pose
very significant challenges for Fonterra. They  also raise some very serious issues, of
course, for the other smaller dairy companies,  and we must never overlook the fact that
some of these so-called smaller companies are small only in relation to Fonterra; they
are quite significant companies by normal New Zealand company standards. Also, these
events pose significant challenges for our scientists and for the members of our
community.
I think we realise that so many questions are being raised for which there are not
adequate answers, but we have tried to fo llow what I call a very segmented and, I think,
logical, approach to handling these issues. By  doing so, I do want to emphasise that this
does not mean that we do not understand th e public clamour and the legitimate public
need for answers to these que stions—I would not use the term “second-tier” questions,
because they are probably fundamentally impor tant questions—but they are issues that
we can come to later, when we have the luxury of time, after dealing with the immediate
issue, which we simply cannot put aside.
We all know—I know that every member of  this House would share this view—that
the immediate issue is the safety  not just of our infants but of infants in other countries.
I think it is a very important thing to co mmunicate beyond, because people are listening
to what we are saying, very carefully. We are just as c oncerned about the infants of
other countries who depend on the safety of the food we send them. I know that I am
speaking on behalf of every sing le member of the House when I say that. That is a very
important point because there will be misleadin g media reports that will play on this. I
think it is very important that this House put s that firmly on the r ecord. That has to be,
frankly, the only real concern.
Of course, in terms of my own responsib ilities, I have got other major economic
concerns in the back of my head, but I do not  think they are separate. I think that the
7 Aug 2013 General Debate 12447
way in which we handle what I call the imme diate issue at hand, th e first-order issue—
which is to find out where potentially contaminated powders may be, remove them from
the market place in all the countries concerne d, and deal with any health consequences
that may arise; and thank God nothing ha s happened so far—will determine some
longer-term responses. Our ability  to deal with the first-order issue will be a matter of
substance. I have been saying on several occas ions over the last few hours that this is
not something that is going to be handled  by slick public relations, photo opportunities,
and such matters; this is something that is  going to be handled by real substance and
professionalism. I think it is very important that we have that firmly in mind.
In respect of the overseas responses, I have not received any information today. I
have heard one story, which I am now told  is incorrect, about Sri Lanka imposing
measures. I am told that is not correct, a nd, obviously, I need to  see this chapter and
verse. There is still the potential for additional import restrictions, new testing measures,
and so on and so forth, because the other regulatory authorities have got the same moral,
legal, and political responsibilities to protect  their people in a situation of uncertainty.
We have to accept that we are not yet fully  in a position—I think we are moving into
this position—to give those regulatory author ities the assurances that they absolutely
need. It may well happen that the web of restri ctions increases, but so far it is only in
China, and I think we have to recognise the incredible professionalism of the Chinese
regulatory authorities in taking such a measured approach, which is focused just on the
actual problem at hand.
I hope that the dairy farmers of New Z ealand, their families, and the communities
that depend so much on their livelihoods  do appreciate what the Chinese regulatory
authorities have done. I think we have a lot to be grateful for, frankly, in the way that
regulatory authorities have responded. Th at may change, we accept that that may
change, and we should accept that as reasonabl e if it does change, and then work away
at resolving those issues with solid, professionally delivered information and data.
Obviously, this will leave a series of other steps that we need to reflect on, and then
develop policy responses. We clearly will need—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Your time has expired.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: One of the ongoing sources of anger and frustration in
my community about the management of the Pike River disaster is that it was the police
who took the lead in managi ng the response to the disast er and who, along with Peter
Whittall from the Pike River Coal compa ny, had responsibility for communicating with
the families and with the public. If it had been the Mines Rescue service in charge,
telling the public that it was not safe to go back into the mine, then people would have
believed it and would not be angry now, at least about that issue. People understand that
Mines Rescue is expert in re scuing people from mines, and they do not expect police to
be. People know that Mines Rescue has no conflict of interest, and they trust it.
So although I agree with much of what Ti m Groser has just to ld the House about
managing this latest issue about contamin ation of whey powder, when it comes to
managing the health consequences of that i ssue—and, rather than the 72 hours that Tim
Groser has just mentioned, actually it is 15 months—and giving parents the information
and advice they desperately need, a Gove rnment that knew what it was doing would
have the Ministry of Health leading a majo r public campaign akin to the one that the
ministry ran on swine flu, for example. It is the chief medical adviser or the Director of
Public Health who needs to be seen talking about this on our television screens every
night and in leaflets on every supermarket shelf, not the act ing Director-General of the
Ministry for Primary Industries.
Various Ministers in the House yester day and, indeed, today were obviously
defensive about this issue, reassuring us th at the Ministry of Health had been involved
12448 General Debate 7 Aug 2013
from the very start. Someone—and I do not  recall which Minister it was—even
mentioned that they remembered the director-general speaking at one of these meetings,
as if that in itself were reassuring to us. With respect, that is not the point.
Even if the chief medical adviser were giving exactly the same information and
advice as the Ministry for Primary Industr ies has been giving, th at would be more
reassuring to the public. That is because when  people need advice about a health issue,
they want to hear it from health experts, not  primary industry experts. It is also because
the Ministry of Health will be trusted as a source of information and advice, whereas the
public understands that both Fonterra, the company responsible for the situation, and the
Ministry for Primary Industries, the Govern ment agency responsible for regulating the
industry and on whose watch this disaster  occurred, have unavoidable conflicts of
interest.
This mistaken response to the health c onsequences goes to the heart of a wider
problem about this Government. As exemplifie d by the lead role that has been played
by the “Minister for Obfuscation and Diversions”, Steven Joyce, this Government’s first
instinct—as it has been with the seri es of scandals around the Government
Communications Security Bureau and the Henry inquiry, for example—is to manage
the political consequences through covering up and distra ctions. Managing the human
consequences seems to be an afterthought.
So when John Key talks about an inquiry a nd getting to the bottom of things, I have
no faith that that is actually his intent, a nd I cannot help but recall the Department of
Labour’s failure to even investigate whether its own actions in respect of Pike River met
the Government’s legal obligations. When this Government talks about a hands-off
approach to regulating indus try, the Green Party stands instead for regulation, for
transparency, and for honest politics. We need the Ministry of Health on the front end of
this issue, and even a white coat would help.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I follow on from the Hon Tim
Groser and the Hon Nathan Guy in reflecting on the incident relating to the potential
contamination of whey products. The first thing I would say and that all members
would, I think, agree with is that we understa nd how serious this is. That is why from
the moment the Government was informed we have swung into action. There have been
many streams of work. The first has been ar ound ensuring that the public is protected.
What has been frustrating, as has been men tioned by a number of my colleagues, is that
the information did change. But what I can tell the mums and dads of New Zealand is
that we have put significant resource into supporting the co mpany that did the recall, to
ensure that the public information campaign is there. We have committed money to that,
and we are doing that.
The second thing I want to reassure the public  about is that the Director-General of
Health and the rest of the response team, wh ich covers the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
and Trade, the Ministry of Health, and a number of other Government agencies, have
been working hard to try to resolve this incident. It has been hard because of the
changing nature of that information, but what I want to assure people about is that today
the director-general will be giving an update on the issues of traceability and
verification, which, I believe, is really impor tant to ensuring that  people have that
confidence. This is a time when the Government needs to operate on a few fundamental
principles, and I believe that we have show n those principles. They are protecting the
public, and they are transparency and openness,  but also doing everyt hing that we can,
regardless of what has been presented to us, to  ensure as much certainty as possible. So
there is a process under way that the Ministry for Primary Industries is focused on.
The other important point that has been raised by the Prime Minister and a number of
other Ministers is that we understand that for a country th at for generations has been
7 Aug 2013 General Debate 12449
providing safe food, this is a serious incident because it doe s dent people’s confidence
in us. That is why we are committed to asking those questions, at the appropriate point,
and to putting a process in place to ensure  that all New Zeala nders, but also people
across the world, have that same level of confidence in our food safety systems.
What I want to do is make this point. The first thing is that our  food safety systems
are made up of significant investment in term s of science, testing, and standards, but I
do believe there are questions that need to be asked, and they will be asked at the
appropriate time. What is important to me are a couple of things. One is ensuring that
the parents in New Zealand and abroad get the best possible information, when we get
it, to ensure that they can keep their families safe. That is why, whether it is through the
social media campaign, the newspaper advertisin g that is planned, or radio advertising,
we are doing everything we can to support that company to  get that information out
there. Also, obviously, the moment that this  was informed to us, we began getting
information to posts in other countries to ensu re that their regulators could do what they
could to protect the families abroad. I think that is a really important point.
It has been a difficult time. I am confid ent that we will rebound from this. I do
believe that the Government has shown an incredible amount of fortitude in terms of the
number of Ministers who have  been involved and have worked really hard across the
Government to do everything we can to mitigate this incident. I just want to reassure the
people of New Zealand that not only do we take it seriously but we are focused on
protecting the public. When the appropriate time happens, we will ensure that those
questions are answered so that we can conti nue to retain our reput ation as one of the
most trusted nations in the world in terms of food. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: Kia orana. Based on what other parliamentarians
have said this afternoon, I want to briefly follow up on what the Minister for Food
Safety has just said. All parliamentarians in the House today and during the course of
the week would endorse that the major focus at the moment ought to be on the families,
the infants, and, obviously, the households that rely on the product that has developed a
very bleak reputation over recent times. Most  certainly, there are queries and questions
about the institution, an institution that enjoys  an extraordinary level of privilege in the
commercial world of New Zealand and holds an  inordinately important status as the
largest trader of dairy products . These are questions that go to the heart of the economy
and go to the heart of key regions around Ne w Zealand. So, although the health and the
well-being of the mokopunas and the familie s who rely on this product around the
world eclipse everything else , at the appropriate time very  searching questions will be
put forward and answers will be demanded. I will just say that.
Now let us talk about jobs. I heard th e member from Northland, Mike Sabin,
unwisely insult Winston Peters earlier today and say to him that he would not know
about Northland because he never goes there. I have sort of found th at for a first-term
member, I am really disappointed that my  fellow Northlander has turned on Winston
like that. I have got no doubt that as time goes on more senior elements in his own party
are going to say: “Oh, for goodne ss’ sake—don’t say that! We have a sort of different
view about Winston.” Well, Winston has a cl ear view about them—it is Winston Peters
whom I am referring to.
But let us talk about jobs. Northland’s job statistics are bleak. They are bleak because
there is no specific set of policies designed to turn round the regions of New Zealand.
Perversely enough, one of the areas that is goi ng to suffer if we do not completely hop
on top and solve the issues ar ound the growth potential of  our dairy industry is the
regions. Why are the regions starving? Well, in frastructure has been starved in relation
to regions. I am not saying that population concentrations are uni mportant, but look at
where much of the primary produce and look at  where much of the export raw material
12450 General Debate 7 Aug 2013
comes from. It comes from the regions. So  do not undercut KiwiRail for a relatively
small amount of money. From Wairoa and Gi sborne through to Heretaunga, reinvest in
that particular portion of our rail infrastructure. Do not ne glect those regions and treat
those regions as though somehow they are less —that their status as New Zealanders is
less important.
Secondly, a hobby horse of mine: forestry. Why is the Minister for Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery not making it a priority and ensuring that all Crown projects in
respect of the Christchurch re build have as a priority th e utilisation of timber, the
utilisation of wood, as Jim Anderton and Helen Clark did?  That is not to say you
exclude concrete, you exclude steel—although fa r be it from me to become a sudden
authority on carbon footprints, etc. But the reality is that our forestry resource and the
secondary and tertiary products from that reso urce have a great role to play in our own
economy. Neglected by the current Minister—we ll, actually the forestry industry does
not know who the current Minister  is. It realises that Nath an Guy is the Minister for
Primary Industries, but based on the body langua ge of the front bench today he is not
going to last long. Not only will there be lo sses of personnel—and I quite like him; I
met him in the golden oldie Parliamentar y Rugby Team—but I think Horowhenua is
going to see a great deal more of him, unfortunately for Horowhenua.
I want to come back to the forestry res ource. Why not promote wood so that it takes
a place of pride in the $40 billion rebuild, a nd ensure that all major designs and major
architecture work have as a model how tim ber, wood, and associated industries can be
utilised in the Christchurch rebuild to enrich  the forestry sector? It is not necessarily
going to cost an inordinate amount of dough, but it is actually re introducing something
that was there prior to Steven Joyce indi scriminately going through a whole host of
policies that Mr Anderton had left for him to advance on. But with Steven Joyce being
the narrow-minded, partisan know-all that he is, Mr Anderton’s contributions were soon
forgotten about. The final point that I would make—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: No, you have run out of time, unfortunately. You will get
it next week.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: On the Ministry for Primary Industries
receiving notification from Fonterra about a potential contamination issue relating to
whey protein concentrate that had tested pos itive for food poisoning bacteria that could
cause botulism, officials immediately sw ung into action. We in the Government
established a ministerial re sponse team, and a number of briefings, meetings, and
teleconferences have been held over the past couple of days since the issue first came to
the regulator’s attention and was brought to the Government’s  attention. The Ministry
for Primary Industries had staff at Fonterra’s Hautapu plant,  which is the site of the
contamination, conducting testing, and also in  Nutricia’s offices, assisting with the
tracking of infant formula that may cont ain the contaminated whey protein. The
ministry has also put official s into Fonterra’s data centres, with its agreement and full
cooperation, to assist in gett ing absolute clarity on the s ituation as it has unfolded. The
situation continues to remain fluid. Minist ers in this debate and speaking previously
have outlined their response and reaction. The information changed a number of times.
That is why officials and the Government ha ve been taking and will continue to take a
conservative, precautionary approach until we can get absolute clarity over this
situation.
Prices dipped overnight at Font erra’s international dairy au ction, the first to be held
since the dairy giant’s milk formula contamin ation scare—the first time since it became
public—but economists have noted that there should be no cause for alarm. Prices
dipped a modest 2.4 percent, compared with the previous sale 2 weeks ago. The total
volume of products sold at auction did increase, however , to a record 60,587 tonnes,
7 Aug 2013 General Debate 12451
and that was up slightly. So the results conf irmed that there has not been a material
market impact on Fonterra’s prices from the contamination issue, and that international
demand for our dairy products remains strong. That does not let us off the hook in any
way, but it does remind us of the importance of the agricultural sector to the New
Zealand economy.
I will be unashamedly parochial in my next few comments, because the lower South
Island—in particular, the Waita ki electorate—is one of th e major contributors to New
Zealand’s economy based on the agricultural sector. The ongoing economic impact of
farming activities in South Canterbury, No rth Otago, and Central Otago, which are all
areas within my electorate, is significant. Close to home, if I think about my house, it
looks down on the Fonterra milk transfer sta tion. When the milk season is under way,
there is a continual stream of milk tankers from the south and from the north converging
on this milk transfer station in Ōāmaru. That continual stream of milk tankers is running
day and night, 24 hours, transferring the milk to the various milk treatment stations.
If I go up the valley a little bit, the Waitaki Valley 30 years ago was a place of
baron, dry, stony waste. With the introduction of the Upper Waitaki and Lower Waitaki
irrigation companies’ activities, that landscap e has now been transformed. It is green.
There are still sheep. There are still deer. There is still cropping. There is an awful lot of
dairying. With that dairying come things li ke houses up roads. Where there was one
house, there are now 10 houses. With those hous es come kids. Those kids go to school.
Their parents go into town. They go to the supermarket. They go to the rural supply
stores and the vet. The vet comes to them and they go to the vet. The economic activity
that is associated with our dairying industry should not be underestimated.
If I look at the North Otago Irrigati on Co.—10,000 hectares under irrigation—in 5
years, under irrigation, farm expenditure has increased 310 percent. There have been—

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: New Zealanders are an incredibly
forgiving and hard-working people. They will forgive their Government many, many
things. When I go out and talk to people in my  electorate of Rimutaka, what they say to
me is that what they want more than anything else is opportunity. They are willing to
work for a better future for themselves and their families. They want the opportunity to
do so. What they are disappointed in is this Government’s failure to  deliver them that
opportunity.
Every time we see unemploy ment statistics come out that show an upturn in
unemployment, as we did today, New Zealande rs have a right to feel disappointed in
that. As of today there are 153,000 New Zeal anders unemployed. That is not because
they do not want to work. That is not because  they are not willing to go and work. It is
because the jobs are not there for them to go and do. They want to see this Government
take action to ensure that they have the oppor tunities to work and to get ahead. That has
to be the unrelenting focus of any Governme nt, and it certainly will be of a future
Labour Government.
We have already outlined a number of very se nsible ideas that will ensure that we
can get New Zealanders into work. One of th em that I am very proud of is converting
the unemployment benefit into a training subsidy fo r young people. It is far, far better
for us to pay to have young New Zealande rs in jobs and training, giving them
meaningful skills that will lead to future productive and prosperous employment, than
have them rotting away on an unemployment be nefit. That is something that the Labour
Party is committed to, and I am incredibly proud of that policy.
New Zealanders want to work hard so th at they can have, and they can purchase,
their own home. It is a big part of the Ki wi dream. Owning your own home is a big part
of being a New Zealander, and Kiwis know that they need to work for that. They do not
want to have it handed to th em on a plate. They are willing to get out there and work
12452 General Debate 7 Aug 2013
hard for it, to save for it, but they want to get a foot on the ladder. They want to have a
chance. At the moment they are seeing thei r hopes and their pros pects crowded out by
overseas speculators coming in and buying up all the available houses, and they are
seeing a Government that is simply willing to turn a blind eye to those things.
We in the Labour Party are saying that we ack nowledge that it is getting increasingly
difficult, and has been for some time, for Ne w Zealand families to purchase their first
home, and that is something that we, as  a future Government, are committed to
addressing. There are many things  that we will do. There is no silver bullet. It is not
going to be a problem that can be fixed overnight. We are committed to building
100,000 affordable homes to give New Zealanders  a chance to get into  their first home.
We will stop the overseas speculators from coming in and crowding New Zealand
families out of the market, so that people can get on to the housing ladder.
We know that New Zealanders are willing to work for it. New Zealanders are willing
to work hard, but when I go out into my electorate and I meet people who are working
two jobs just to get ahead and they still cannot make ends meet, that means that
something is wrong. They do not have a Government that is willing to back them. This
Government talks about backing people into work, but it will not back them once they
actually get there. There are people who go out there and do a hard day’s labour—and
in many cases they are working evenings, t oo—but who are not getting a pay rate that
adequately compensates them for that, and I do not think that th at is right, either.
Instead, what they have got under this Govern ment is a Government that is committed
to eroding their rights even further, to making life even more difficult for people who
are going out there and working hard to try to get ahead.
New Zealanders will forgive their Government many, many things and they will give
it the benefit of the doubt, but they want to know that the Government that they have
put in place is responsibly exercising the power  and the trust invested in it. They want a
Government that cares about their welfare and their well-being. This Government has
demonstrated in recent years that it will wield the power of the State in order to protect
itself and for its own end. Government memb ers will wield the power of the State to
protect their own privacy. So when the privacy of the Prime Minister and Mr Banks was
being threatened, they did not hesitate to se nd the police in to raid media outlets. They
will wield the power of the State to protect the privacy of Mr Dunne, who is quite happy
to protect his own personal communications whilst voting for a law that removes the
right to privacy for many, many other New Ze alanders. They will wield the power of
the State to protect themselves and thei r own interests, but they are woefully
inadequate—silent, in fact—when it comes to actually protecting the interests of
everyday New Zealanders, who want to go out there, who want to work hard, and who
want to create a better future for themselves and for their families.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: It would be fair to sa y that the issue that we
are confronted with as a nation of managing the contamination scare with the whey was
too close for comfort for any person of this  country, especially any primary producer.
So how do we feel? As a rura l MP myself and as a member on the Primary Production
Committee, I must say that it was a breat htaking moment when we heard the story
break. One can imagine how those people who ha ve got millions of dollars invested in
the primary industries in New Zealand would have felt when that crisis broke. They
were all affected in the sense that mark et access is something that we do value
incredibly highly.
So what was the potential of this breach, of this incursion? When you look at it, more
often than not, what we have in our mind- set is an incursion by a biosecurity breach.
But this was not the case. This was a cas e where potentially one of our own products
was the problem, and we had to work our  way through that. So it was wholly
7 Aug 2013 General Debate 12453
appropriate that the Government moved quickly, as it did, and credit must also go to the
Ministry for Primary Industries. So well done.
What was the appropriate focus that the Government had? The focus and response of
the Government was to protect families, espe cially the babies. As Minister Tim Groser
made the point, it was not only for New Zealand families but especially for our overseas
families. May I acknowledge at this particular  stage the appropriate effort put in by the
Prime Minister, John Key, ably supported by Ministers Joyce, Groser, Guy, Goodhew,
Ryall, and Kaye. Also, the officials got alongside Fonterra’s Hautapu plant so that there
was good information being given to the public. It  is also nice to see presently that, as
the story has unfolded and the facts are es tablished, the process has been described,
from the Government’s point of view, as a class act.
I venture to say that we in New Zeala nd need to examine our processes more
thoroughly. I am confident that this scare and the resulting examination will result in
standards of monitoring that  will get better and better through the process, and we
should welcome that and open ourselves up to such an examination. This reminds me of
a very sage statement that we all in the House will remember: “It is the putting right that
counts.” I believe that that statement is so very important and appropriate. Having
identified the problem, having isolated th e product, we have now got the job of
rebuilding the confidence of our partners—the people whos e countries we export to—
realising that we are the largest cross-border exporter of milk products. We have really
got to work at rebuilding that confidence—the putting right of things.
Churchill also made a very appropriate co mment that “Bad news will travel around
the world before good news even gets its pants on.” That is pretty appropriate when you
consider that it is a matter that we have got to be very consci ous of. Fortunately, the
Government’s response has been to largely k eep up with the developments of this issue
as it has unfolded and, fortunately, New Zealanders have a natural way of doing
business overseas as an expor t nation. Our officials are open and transparent, and they,
along with other Government officials, will work really diligently and hard to make sure
that that trust is rebuilt.
There is a need for inquiries. These inquiri es will add robustness to our food safety
systems, and it is very important that that is  the case and that we restore the brand value
to the New Zealand brand.
To conclude, I would just like to address the farmers of New Zealand in the sense
that there have been times in  the recent past when this Government has put in place
necessary regulation and legisla tion that has made farmers a little bit irate. They feel
that we are adding cost to their farmi ng systems without adding value, and I am
referring there to the National Animal Id entification and Tracing Act. I would just
encourage farmers to focus on the fact that this is very important for biosecurity and
food safety. Thank you.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: Kia orana, Mr Deputy Speaker. Nobody can
deny the seriousness of the food safety situati on that New Zealand fi nds itself in, and I
do want to acknowledge that. I also want to acknowledge another very serious matter, a
matter of vital concern to Ne w Zealanders, and that is th e need for decent jobs and
decent incomes—something that this Government  ignores. This is a Government that is
out of touch and a Prime Mini ster who is deeply bogged do wn in covering his tracks
again. This time it is on the Dunne email scandal and the Government Communications
Security Bureau debacle, which is someth ing that New Zealander of the Year Anne
Salmond has been quite vocal about and has described as a massive breach of trust
between Parliament and its citizens.
Today we have seen unemployment increase , up from 6.2 percent last quarter to 6.4
percent today—that is, 48,000 more people ar e unemployed now than when National
12454 General Debate 7 Aug 2013
took office in 2008. In total, 153,0000 Ne w Zealanders—that is right, 153,000—are
unemployed, and almost daily we hear of mo re job losses. There have been significant
job losses all around New Zealand, but jobs and decent incomes are, in fact, the only
way forward for New Zealanders. As others  have said, New Zealanders are committed
to the idea of working hard to get ahead for an opportunity for their family—a fair day’s
work for a fair day’s pay. These are basic New Zealand principles. Jobs are the way that
most New Zealanders sustain a decent stan dard of living for themselves and their
family. They are a way for them to contribute  their ideas and their labour to grow our
economy and to participate in our community.
But our Prime Minister is more focuse d on denying responsib ility for anything
negative. He constantly is blaming somebody else—blaming Labour—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: That’s right.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: —but, in fact, you have been in Government for 5 years, so
take responsibility. The Prime Minister, and th e Government as a w hole, needs to take
responsibility. No longer can you continue to blame the last Government or the global
financial crisis. You need to take responsibil ity and focus on the real  issues: the issues
of jobs and incomes.
But let us look more closely at what is ha ppening to jobs and income, shall we? We
have 153,000 people unemployed, a total of 245,400 people who are jobless, and
another 63,000 people who are wanting extra hou rs of work, and it is a very tough time
to be looking for work. M āori unemployment is at 12.8 percen t, and, actually, that is a
slight reduction, so that is good news. But Pa sifika unemployment has increased to 16.3
percent. Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga was busy crow ing earlier today about the number of jobs
that are on job vacancy websites. Well, I do not think that is going to deal with the 16.3
percent of Pacific people who are unemployed. And what about wages? Well, wages are
up by only 1.7 percent, and the median for those who actually got a pay increase—and
this is the key—was 2.7 percent, which is the lowest increase since 2001. But in the last
year 45 percent of employees received no pay increase at all. At the same time, prices
were skyrocketing, power prices went up, accommodation prices went up, and 45
percent of workers got no pay increase.
So let us get a renewed focus on creating decent jobs for workers. It is no good
saying that the economy is pick ing up if that benefit is not flowing through to wages
and jobs. Our wages remain 34 percent lowe r than in Australia, and yet we have a
Government introducing legi slation that will drive wages down further. The
Employment Relations Amendment Bill will drive wages down even further, so we
need to do more. We need to do more to focus on growing the number of jobs. The
Government needs to take responsibility, but we do not believe that it will. It is going to
take a Labour Government to get a focus on jobs and on putting in place a really hands-
on approach towards job crea tion, and to invest in lifel ong learning and upskilling.
Members opposite, your Government promised  in 2011 that it w ould create 170,000
jobs by 2015—170,000 jobs by 2015. Well, so far that is 1,700, so you have got a long
way to go—a long way to go.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I have an opportunity  to stand here for
the second time this week to support this Government’s efforts to ensure that our
worldwide reputation does not suffer undue damage as a result of Fonterra’s potential
whey contamination matter. I would say, just befo re I get into what I want to say, that I
want to disappoint one of th e previous speakers, Shane Jones. He will, for many years
to come, have to put up with Minister Guy and Mike Sabin, whether he likes it or not,
and I shall remind him of that in the future.
I think we can be pretty proud of the fact that Fonterra has been able, firstly, to
identify the problem and, secondly, to trace it.  I do not for a moment believe that every
7 Aug 2013 General Debate 12455
company in the world could have achieved this. I also want to commend our team of
Ministers for a very competent response to a very serious situation for New Zealand and
for New Zealanders. Having said that, I do not underestimate the seriousness of the
situation for Fonterra as one of our top f ood producers, for the farmer-shareholders, for
the country, and, most critical ly, for the international an d national consumers—notably,
the children and calves, who are the most likely consumers of these recalled products.
No other country in the world has the reliance on food quality, safety, and quantity
that we have, and there is no place on earth where food safety is more important than
here in New Zealand. We have traversed many miles in the past few years in respect of
food safety, but it is clear from the occurrences of the last week that we still have some
way to go. I want to spend some time talki ng about the miles we have travelled and
some of the challenges we face as a nation.
In New Zealand we know where the calf I referred to earlier was born, where it
travels to, and where it is processed, pack ed, shipped, and eaten. The challenge for our
food industry—as with medicine, for example— is that the recipe contains so many
ingredients. What we have to ensure is that all of those are safe and that the subsequent
mixture—the chemistry, so to speak—is compatible. This was, of course, the challenge
that Fonterra and the Ministry for Primar y Industries faced with the whey protein
product. It is used in many hundreds of mixtures throughout th e world. It is
manufactured in New Zealand but then travels all over the world. There is no doubt that
this is a great challenge to New Zealand, because many of our other products are in
exactly the same situation.
We heard Labour’s agriculture  spokesman yesterday and its leader today talking
about inadequate funding within  the food safety division of the Ministry for Primary
Industries. I want to counter this because I think it is irresponsible. As they both should
know, issues of national sign ificance will always be funded and always have been
funded, and New Zealand will always be in a position to fund them. They should also
know, if they have read their books properly, that the cuts to the ministry have not been
made to the food safety division’s front-line operations. I would also  add that I do not
believe that a witch-hunt at this stage w ould serve any purpose, and the subsequent
inquiries, which are necessary, will reveal all of the necessary information to allow us to
move on and ensure that these types of food safety issues do not arise in the future.
My electorate of Rangit īkei is a farming electorate. We rely heavily on our
producers of meat, milk, vegetables, fruit, even some fish—mostly  eels, actually—and
honey for our living. Animal welfare and food safety are critical to us in the Rangit īkei.
We have three large meat plants, a veni son processing plant, two milk plants—a
Fonterra and a Goodman Fielder plant— and a number of highly technical,
pharmaceutical-type manufacturers, includi ng New Zealand Pharmaceuticals and the
recently announced Proliant plant, which is  moving to Feilding. We are doing well in
this country at present, w ith more jobs and better syst ems, services, and household
incomes. We must ensure that this continue s. Food safety, animal welfare, and better
productivity will be vital to our futures in New Zealand. Thank you.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
