items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: We are all familiar with the adage that those who fail
to learn from history are doomed to repeat  it. Sadly, the drafting of this bill, the
Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill, and those people who are
supporting this bill today are demonstrating th eir inability to learn from, indeed, quite
recent history—10 or 15 years of history. Th e lessons have not been learnt. The key
lesson that has evidently not been learnt is  that one-off, narrowly focused pieces of
legislation are not the solution to complex, multifaceted social problems, or to the
manifestations of those problems. It is not a difficult proposition. It is one that has been
demonstrated repeatedly, even as recently as since the early and mid-1990s, that one-off
legislative fixes will not be sufficient to  deal with complex social problems. Mr
Mitchell has admitted that this is not a silver bullet. Sadly, it is not any sort of a bullet.
At best it is a blunt instrument. Nati onal members might get some superficial
satisfaction, or perhaps even a degree of short-term political advantage, from seeing one
or two gang members arrested for either de liberately or accidentally contravening this
law, because given the farcical nature of some of the provisions of this law it would
actually be quite easy to ac cidentally contravene this law. I support Mr Goff’s
comments about the lack of consistency, the lack of clarity, in it.
But to return to the key point, we need to look at long-term solutions. We need to
deal with the root causes of crime and offe nding, and we need to l ook at the drivers of
why we have gangs, why gangs are manifes ting in our communities, and why they are
so embedded in some communities. I see it  close up and personal in Northland,
Kaikohe, Moerewa, and Kait āia. They are small towns in Northland where gangs are
prevalent and where they are influential —very often in a negative way, although not
always. We do need to address the issues and the problems associated with their
behaviours. This bill does not even begin to go anywhere near a ddressing the causes of
the offending and of the existence of these organisations.
A whole raft of legislation went through this House in the early to mid-1990s, driven
by a moral panic that largely came out of this debate about who is hard, who is tough on
crime, and who is soft on crime. I have to say that sitting here watching that interchange
of points of order recently about who is tough on crime, soft on crime, and who is a
petal—really, we need to get beyond that. Tough on crime, soft on crime? How about
we be smart on crime? Let us think about smart solutions—21 st century, real solutions
to crime, to the problems of gangs in our co mmunities, and to the social behaviours that
come alongside that. The lesson of the 1990s, which clearly has not been learnt by some
members of this House, is that legislativ e solutions seldom gene rate any measurable,
positive outcomes. We had law passed about criminal association. We had law that
enabled local authorities and police to knock down gang fo rtifications. We saw changes
to the liquor law. None of these had any m easurable or discernible effect on the long-
term, deeply seated, complex problems about gang membership, gangs in our
communities, and the criminal offending associated with those problems. Why do we
not actually want to address the real underl ying problems? Mr F aafoi has touched on
some of those, which are unemployment, social disadvantage, and alienation.
I have made this recommendation in an earl ier speech on this bill, but I would again
recommend that members of the Government parties, particularly, get hold of a book
called Patched by Jarrod Gilbert, which presents evid ence and presents a social history
of gangs in New Zealand. It points out that gangs in some form or another have been
12478 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 7 Aug 2013
around at least since the 1950s . Typically, they were gr oups of young men, alienated
and rebellious. They joined a gang, got themselves into mischief and trouble for a few
years, and then essentially grew out of it. They would go and get themselves a job, they
would marry, and they would get a house. The patched gangs that are now the cause or
the target of this bill are an unusual pheno menon, in that rather than the members of
those gangs joining for a few years and then  thinking better of it, discovering there
would be better ways to spend their lives than bouncing in and out of trouble with the
police and jail, and getting on with life in a much more communally acceptable way, the
difference for those gang members is, of c ourse, that the 1980s—through the misguided
new-right policies of the 1980s—entrenched unemployment.
We are now seeing second and third-generation unemployment and second and third-
generation gang membership. It is not hard to join the dots, to look at the causal links
between those—the attack on th e structure and the fabric of New Zealand society as it
was prior to the new-right so-called revolution of the 1990s and carried on into the
2000s, and the fact that we have now got these embedded memberships, the
multigenerational memberships, of gangs. Th at is a very, very difficult problem to
overcome and to address. We will not do it by little bits of one-off legislation that put
some very limited constraints on the gang movements and behaviours of members of
gangs.
I would almost guarantee, I would almost be willing to wager, that there will be legal
challenges to this legislation once it is pass ed. It will be exactly as we saw in the
Whanganui gang patch legislation, where me mbers of Hell’s Angels deliberately
walked around outside the poli ce station, flaunting gang in signia. They got themselves
arrested and not only went to court but act ually won the court case, which gave great
comfort and added to the mana of gangs, rath er than diminishing it or taking away from
it. Again, I think there is a lesson there that has not been learnt. I will wager that there
will be legal challenges to this bill, and pr obably successful legal challenges, based on
all sorts of interesting legal propositions that we have yet to see or hear.
I have to say, this very day at lunchtime, just next door in the Grand Hall, there was a
launch of the Justice Coalition, which is a cluster of progressive NGOs around the
justice sector that have come together w ith common cause to endeavour to offer good
solutions to the problems of crime, offending, imprisonment, and all of the other bundle
of justice issues, if you like. I must say in passing that the Minist er of Corrections was
there, and she announced a very positive policy to have an education strategy for every
single inmate in our prisons. I commend the Mi nister on that. We will look with interest
to ensure that th e policy as it is on paper is reinforced with  resources and funding to
make it succeed. That is an example, actually, of a bit of joined-up thinking about
criminal offending and prisons, and some of th e solutions to them. It is a mile away
from the sort of nonsense that we are seeing in the bill we are debating today.
I was interested to see how few National MP s were present at that launch. In fact,
other than the Minister, I do not believe that  I saw one. I did see Labour members there,
and Green members were present. It is unf ortunate that some of the Government
members supporting this bill were not at th at launch. I recommend to them that they
have a look and learn a little  about the Justice Coalition,  which bases its operations,
among other things, on having a vision about what sort of a New Zealand we want. It
has an idea that any legislation or policy s hould have measurable outcomes. It suggests
that justice legislation and justice policy s hould be evidence-based. I would challenge
anybody to put this piece of legislation through that filter. Is it vi sionary? Will there be
measurable outcomes from it? Is it evidence -based? I would suggest  that it would fail
on all of those measures. It would fail on that filtering, if you like.
7 Aug 2013 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 12479
Tough on crime, soft on crime—let us be smart on crime. Let us look for real
solutions that we know will work. They are complex and they are multifaceted. They
will require us to spend money differently. We do not have to spend more money on
justice; we just need to spend it differently. We need to engage with the communities. In
the drafting of this bill, did anybody go out and talk to the gang members about their
behaviours, and ask them what  it would take for them to  not behave in these ways?
Believe it or not, there are some intelligen t thinkers in the gangs. Some of the older
gang members have turned a corner. They re alise the error of their ways. They have
joined things like the White Ribbon campaign and some of the anti-violence and anti-
drug movements. There is hope by working collaboratively and engaging with these
offenders and former offenders, rather than pr etending that these little one-off pieces of
legislation will have any positive effect or a ny positive outcome at all. It will chew up
police time. No doubt it will l ead to a few arrests. It wi ll lead to legal challenges.
Ultimately, it will even lead to enhancing the mana of the gangs, as I have said. It will
become a point of pride to have one’s gang named in this legislation. This is a very poor
piece of legislation. The Greens will continue to oppose it.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I do not know what  it is about the
Greens, but every time they speak in this House, it reminds me of that song that goes:
“Oh Lord it’s hard to be humble, when you’re  perfect in every way”, because, clearly,
they have been here for 20-odd years and have never had to put their heads on the block.
I just want to comment on the fact that th is bill, the Prohibition of Gang Insignia in
Government Premises Bill, really has been a fascinating study of the legislative process
in action. No legislation in this House will ev er be perfect. No legi slation that can ever
be passed will be perfect. No legislation ha s ever solved all the problems in their
entirety. This piece of work is no exception. But contrary to the protestations of Labour,
and clearly now David Clendon, it will make a difference. It will put some curbs on the
activities of gangs. It will give our police fo rce another tool in their armoury. It will
give some peace of mind to those people working on the front line of our public
services. It will give them some protecti on from intimidation—the intimidation caused
when a patched gang member leans on the count er, demanding service. I have seen it. I
have seen it in public sector buildings, I have  seen it in councils, and it is not pleasant.
The bill will enable our schools to ban patches from their grounds.
The gang insignia bill was introduced to this House from the members’ ballot by the
now Hon Todd McClay in respon se to issues that were a ffecting his electorate. Todd
McClay then became a Minister and passed the bill to one of our ex-coppers, Mark
Mitchell. Who better to steer this bill through the House? Who knows better than an ex-
copper the damage these gangs cause to our communities?
This bill falls clearly into the orbit of the Law and Order Committee, and further
complements the great result that this Government has achieved through Ministers
Tolley, Collins, and Borrows, and, form erly, Simon Power. The Law and Order
Committee, by select committee standards I ha ve witnessed in this House, operates
pretty well. It operates unde r a very good chair and an equa lly good deputy chair, and,
frankly, we would normally have a very good relationship with the other members of
that select committee as well. We generally do not cause Phil Goff to have to shout
quite as loudly as he was shouting in this House earlier in the day.
The results of the law and order policies of  this Government have been spectacular.
There has been a 30 percent drop in youth crime, a fantastic improvement in police
resources through the use of  technology on the beat—up t o, in fact, Feilding police
station having a saving of 20 percent of th e total force in Feilding’s time. That has
happened in about 8 months.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: That’s because you’ve got fewer cops.
12480 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 7 Aug 2013

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: We listen to Mr Faafoi bleating on about the reduction in the
police budget, but those figures make a nonsense of that. We have also seen—

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: I’ll table them, then. They’re the Minister’s figures.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: You are most certainly welcome to table them. We have also
seen vastly improved rehabilitation and retr aining of prisoners, which is making a big
difference to the future of those people. Th ese initiatives and achievements complement
the further introduction of legislation in th is area, including the Bail Amendment Bill,
the Juries (Jury Service and Protection of Particulars of  Jury List Information)
Amendment Bill, the Administration of Community Sentences and Orders Bill, the
Corrections Amendment Bill, and many more. The gang insignia bill sits right alongside
those as another tool in the tool box of the New Zealand Police.
Crime is an insidious thing. It can have a dramatic effect on a victim. Equally, it can
go unnoticed for years. Crime in our commu nities is often inflicted on the most
vulnerable in our society. You see, criminals are bullies. They do not pick on those who
can fight back. Does that not remind you or me—in fact, apologies, Mr Deputy Speaker,
I am not trying to remind you. Does that not  remind us of a gang member? They are
bullies, and that is what they make their livelihoods from. That is what they spend their
lives doing—bullying people.
I just want to very briefly comment on Mr  Goff’s comments on this bill, because I
cannot believe that someone with his vast  experience of inep t lawmaking can now
criticise a Government member for bringing a bill to this House and say it is inept
lawmaking. It is inevitable in the course of making any law that you are going to have
inept lawmakers; people whose law does not achieve what it initially set out to do. I
think that everyone who brings legislation or proposals to this House, particularly
members who bring them through the members’ bills process, bring them here with the
best intentions. I do not think it is our busin ess to necessarily pull those people apart for
the manner in which they do that.
Intimidating public servants, people who work for our Government and cannot dodge
people, is not a pleasant way to be. In the private sector we can do what we want with
those people. We can deal with them as we like. We can ban them. We can trespass
them. We do not have to serve them. In the public sector our public servants cannot do
that. At Work and Income, at post offices, at  hospitals, and at schools they have got to
look after those people.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: You can trespass them.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: You may be able to trespass them but you need to look after
those people, because that is what we are here for. That is what Governments are for. So
bill this will give public servants a little bit of an opportunity to manage that a bit better.
I want to briefly address Mr Faafoi’s P acific unemployment issue. In Marton, which
is a town in my electorate, I have about 30 to 40 Samoan families a year coming into
this country to work in the meat company just down the road. That happens every year,
so I fail to understand why, in places like the Rangit īkei electorate, large numbers of
Pacific Islanders are coming into the countr y to work, and at the other end we have
them dropping out of the workforce. That is something we need to address.
Before I finish I also want to comment on the latest edition of the Listener, which I
notice is red and has got “risk” written all over it. I suspect that is where we are at.
Thank you.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: It is with a great deal of satisfaction that I rise to
stand in support of this Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill. New
Zealand First is proud to support this bill. We are proud to stand in support of this fine
bill, which is about to become a splendid law.  We have been here from the outset, from
the beginning, when Mr McClay introduced his member’s bill; through its first and
7 Aug 2013 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 12481
second readings; through the Committee stage,  when we were able to contribute
constructively to the bill and when the G overnment most generously chose to embrace
the spirit of cooperation that New Z ealand First brought to it by supporting
Supplementary Order Paper 253, which was in my name; through the handover, when
the newly promoted Minister McClay passed the baton to Mr Mitchell, who, in turn, has
ably shepherded the bill through to its conclu sion—and so we arrive. We arrive at the
culmination of this process of lawmaking by which an inspired thought has given life,
when one man’s righteous indignation at a pe rceived injustice grows from the spark of
contemplation to become something tangible,  and when it grows to become the law of
the land.
This law will be a tool, a weapon, in the ha nds of our police, and a device by which
they may remove the scourge of gangs and of gang members from the eye and the
presence of decent people and decent society. That splinter of one man’s mind’s eye has
grown to be a shaft of light breaking through the darkness that is the gangs and the gang
culture in this country, growing to become a sabre of justice in the hands of our law
enforcement officers, and a sword of Damocles hanging over the heads of the gangs and
their filthy and abhorrent lives and behaviour.
The passing of this bill marks the e nding of one process and the beginning of
another. We are witness, we here in this H ouse are witness, to the dawn of a new time.
This bill and its passing into law mark the beginning of the end for the gangs and the
gang culture in New Zealand. Through this bill, and through the others that will
follow—the laws that are yet to come but whic h will follow in the wake of the trail that
this bill has blazed—we will see the gangs expunged from the fabric of New Zealand
life and society. We stand in the dawning of  the light of a new day. The darkness is
ending. The gangs should be afraid. They should be very afraid. We, the decent people
of New Zealand, are claiming back the night. We are claiming back the streets. We are
claiming back the rule of law. The gangs will  be consigned to hist ory and they will be
driven back. They will be forced to crawl or  scuttle or slither ba ck under the rocks and
the rotting logs where they belong, back to the shadows from whence they came. That
shadow will be lifted. That veil of darkness that the gangs have held over New Zealand
for these past 40 years will be torn away by this bill and by the others that will follow in
its wake.
I think it is fitting for us to remember to pay tribute to those who have lived and who
continue to live under that shadow. The dark criminality of the gangs has been a curse
on too many people’s lives. Too many good peopl e have been defiled and despoiled by
the evil filth of gangs, gang members, gang culture, and gang crime. In the mean streets
of too many of our cities and towns, th ere are people—good, ordi nary citizens and
families—living in fear of the gangs and thei r intimidation, their th reats, both real and
implied, their presence, and the very real power over people, denoted by the displaying
of the patch. Well, no longer. This bill will put an end to that intimidation. In time it
will put an end to that threat, an end to th e threat against the safety of good, ordinary
people, and an end to the threat against the safety of our police o fficers, who serve and
protect us all.
Mr Mitchell, himself a former police officer, and others from the Government side of
the House have reminded us more than once of what the gang patch stands for. They
have not let us forget that th e patch is the mark of a criminal, that its awarding denotes
the commission of the vilest of crimes against innocent people—robbery, rape, and
murder—committed for their own sake as much as for personal gain, committed to
demonstrate to their fellow lowlifes and repr obates that they are worthy of the patch,
which until now they have worn as a ba dge of honour but which will now become a
badge of shame.
12482 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 7 Aug 2013
We owe a great deal to the brave and honourable men and women who wear the blue
uniform. This bill and the law that it is about to become will give them a new and
powerful tool with which to remove the ugly menace of the gangs from our cities,
towns, and streets; to remove their presence  and their intimidation;  and to bring an end
to the drugs, the crime, and the violen ce that are visited upon good people by the evil
that is the gangs. The police in New Zealand welcome this bill. They welcome this new
tool, and we in New Zealand First are delighted  to have been able to play a hand in
helping to craft it and in helping to ensure its passage through this House and into law.
So we come to an end and to a beginning. I look forward to the grim satisfaction that
I am sure we will all feel—all of us who st and in support of this bill, and, I suspect,
more than a few of those who profess not to—when the first gang patch to be
confiscated under this new law is consigned to its doom in a police incinerator. May
that flame, may the fire of a burning gang patch, serve as a beacon—the flame of justice
casting aside the forces of dar kness with the light of civilis ation. May that light lift the
shadow of the gangs from the lives of all the good and innocent pe ople who have lived
and who continue to live under their menace. I look forward to that day.
In closing, then, I say to the members of th is House that we in New Zealand First are
proud to support this bi ll. We are proud to stand with al l those who hold the rights of
good and innocent people up above those of crim inals and lowlifes. This is a fine bill
and it will be a fine law.  We welcome it, we support it, and we commend it to the
House. Thank you.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I do not know quite how to follow that
contribution, that fine Churchillian c ontribution, by the member opposite, Richard
Prosser, delivered with such passion. But is that not what this House is all about? Is that
not what this bill is all about? Is not this  Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government
Premises Bill about New Zealand society caring enough to do something about a part of
our society that causes unending problems and heartache for some people? So I want to
congratulate Richard Prosser. He has entert ained us. It was a wonderful speech, but the
point is that he is absolutely  right. I am so pleased that New Zealand First is supporting
the bill in the name of Mark Mitchell, because it is a bill that deserves to be supported.
The board of trustees from Murupara  Area School came to the Law and Order
Committee and made some very strong points to us. What they said was that they loved
their school as parents and tr ustees and community members.  They loved their school,
they loved their children, and they loved their community. They wanted nothing more
for their community than for their children to be able to go to school, enjoy their time at
school, learn, and then get home safely. That is  what we all want for our children. The
problem is that in Murupara they could not  do that. Why? Because of the influence of
the gangs in the community. That influence wa s reaching not just through the streets of
the town but right into the school, right into  the playground, and they wanted to put a
stop to it. It is as simple as that. That community, that school community, wanted to put
a stop to the intimidation of gangs in thei r community, so they came to our committee,
the Law and Order Committee, in support of th is bill. They came to our Law and Order
Committee in support of giving police the power  to seize without warrant gang patches
of gang members and then, if the gang memb ers were to be found guilty, to have the
patches destroyed. The police support this bill because they know—they know—that
the gang patch is the badge of honour for th ese people. Taking away that badge of
honour leaves them with what? It leaves th em with nothing. And that is where we
should be with these people in New Zealand.
What has been so terribly difficult for the Labour members opposite is that they have
found themselves in a trap of  having to oppose everything just because they are the
Opposition. Members like Phil Goff and Kris Faafoi have found themselves in the
7 Aug 2013 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 12483
position of having to oppose something that  they know fundamentally is a good
measure and is welcomed throughout sectors like the police and like communities that
really know and understand the impact that gangs have on them. Labour members have
found themselves in this awkw ard position of having to find reasons to oppose the bill.
So we have had Phil Goff canvassing that pe rhaps the bill is ridiculous because you
could walk along a walkway but wh at if it has a roof? Well, OK, let us just tighten up
the definition in the bill. That is no reason to oppose it. It must have been very awkward
for Kris Faafoi when members of the Wh itireia Community Law Centre from Porirua
came to the committee in support of this bill for very good reason. It must have been
very difficult for Kris Faafoi to keep oppos ing this bill, when his own constituents—his
own constituents, his own community—cam e to the Law and Order Committee in
support of this bill.
I am proud of this bill. I think Todd McClay did exactly the right thing in introducing
this bill to the House. I think the bill ha s been well taken up by his colleague Mark
Mitchell, who is also a man who understands fundamentally that the measures in this
bill will go a long way to addressing the probl em of gangs in New Zealand. Of course it
is not going to fix the problem—Richard Prosse r wants it to, we all want it to, and good
on him for expressing that thought —but it will send a message in the strongest terms to
the gangs of New Zealand that enough is enough and that this Parliament takes the issue
seriously. I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I rise to take a call on this third reading of the
Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Prem ises Bill. I want to say of the member
responsible for this bill, Mark  Mitchell, that he has very quickly in his time in this
House—the same time as I have spent in th is House—become one of the respected and
sensible members of the National Party. Th e National Party does not have many, so it
has got to hang on to the ones it has got. But the truth is that he has been given a
hospital pass on this bill, because deep in his heart of hearts, I know, I am confident, he
knows that this is a half measure, it is a non-measure, and it will not achieve half the
things that some of the speakers on the other side of the House have claimed of it. The
last speaker, Jacqui Dean, claimed all sorts of things that this bill was going to do, and
that we just had to tweak a bit here and tweak a bit there. Well, we are past the tweaking
stage. This is it. This is the bill. The time of this House is being called upon to pass this
bill in its current form —the current meaningless, ineffective, hopeless form that it is in.
It simply will not do those things.
I could not go further without  acknowledging the words of  Richard Prosser, whose
torch is obviously burning very  brightly tonight. His dream, clearly, is of dancing with
Anne Tolley around the beacons of hope fo r peace and good order, and dancing on the
crushed vehicles, the stomping softened onl y by the leather obtained from the seized
patches of gang members. Well, we can all ha ve that dream. We have those sorts of
dreams every now and again—or at least some  people do. I want to put out to Mr
Prosser, however, that a burka is not a gang patch. So the bill is not going to fulfil some
of his personal ambitions in that regard.
The truth about this bill is that those in control of Government premises can already
take action, meaningful action, and there is ample evidence before the House and that
went before the Law and Order Committee to suggest that. The last time I spoke on this
bill, in the Committee stage, I adduced  as evidence a copy of that day’s New Zealand
Herald, that august publication. It had the wit at that time to publish a photograph of the
Napier District Court, and in that photograph of the Na pier District Court entrance was
a little sign that said “No gang patches in this building”. Here it was, a Government
building, a little sign saying “No gang patche s in this building”, and the report said,
12484 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 7 Aug 2013
amongst other things, that there were no problems with gangs in that building. It was all
done without the benefit of this legislation.
Then we had the evidence of  the Murupara Area School, which people have spoken
so fondly of in the debate today. It came and spoke in support of the bill, but the truth is
that when you look at the facts of its si tuation, it supports the opposite. The school has
demonstrated that it can banish gangs and gang patches and leather jackets from its
premises without this bill. It did it without the bill. Through good leadership and a good,
strong community, the school demonstrated that  it could take control of its Government
premises without meaningless legislation like this. It can create the culture, it can set the
rules, it can make the standards, it can do it—and it did it. The school community, the
teachers in it, the principal, and, most impor tant, the children in it have now taken
control of their place of learning. It is a good, healthy place to be, and they did it all
without this legislati on. So the truth is that this le gislation will do nothing. This
legislation will do nothing.
Let us be clear too about what it does not cover, because that is just as important. It
will not cover organisations like the National Front.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Well, what an interesting interposition that was. The
fascinating thing was that tonight we saw, as we see most  weeknight evenings, the TV3
news broadcast, and it had two interesting st ories on it. One was about this bill, and the
other was about a cartoon character called th e Burka Avenger. One of the stories was
full of facts and was fascinating and interesting; the other was a complete work of
fiction. It will stun  this House to know  that the story on 3 News  tonight that was a
complete work of fiction was the story abou t this bill. What it did was it gave the
impression to any member of the viewing public that this bill is going to somehow clean
the streets of New Zealand of gang memb ers and those wearing gang patches. We
know, and anyone who has taken a moment to read the bill  will know, that it will do
nothing of the sort.
I might say—bearing in mind that I bega n my contribution tonight mentioning the
burka—that I was very impressed with the Burk a Avenger. If we could have the Burka
Avenger, the avenging Islamic woman, co ming down and cleaning up evil wrongdoers
and all the rest of it, she would have a very important role to play in this country, unlike
this bill—unlike this bill.
The point I was making at th e time of the dinner break wa s that there are plenty of
things that this bill will not  do. For one thing, there are na sty, insidious gangs that this
bill will not go near. One of them is the Na tional Front. Its members wear a uniform, all
right. They wear attachments and wear their hair in certain styles —the skinhead. They
wear tattoos. They wear dark clothing. They  intimidate, they stand over, and they do
evil things, but this bill will not do anything about them, and these people will continue
to turn up in public places and they w ill do their intimidation. They will do their
standover stuff. And all the bleating from the members opposite will not make a tinker’s
cuss of difference to organisations like that.
The reality about the National Party members is  that they come to this House, they
puff out their chests, they sound tough, they talk tough, but they do not know what they
are doing, and they do not ca re. They do not care about the vast majority of New
Zealanders who want to go about their work aday lives in a safe, peaceful community.
They want window dressing. They do window dressing. Whether it is the streets of
Feilding or whether it is the streets of the far north, they will do the window dressing.
That will get them a few point s in the next poll, but it will  not fix the real problems of
New Zealand.
7 Aug 2013 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 12485
So what about particular areas that this  bill covers? Well, it says that it covers
Government premises. What about kids’ pa rks? What about the beach? What about
those places where you go and have a barbecue on a sunny S unday evening? It will not
touch any of those areas. What about city c ouncil - controlled areas like parks that are
full of trees and without a single man-made  structure? Gangs turn up there when
families are trying to have their family picn ics. The bill will not make a blind bit of
difference to that situation or to those people, so the gangs wearing their thuggish
patches can carry on and do their thing.
We all know the problem about gangs, and we  do not shy away from that problem.
We know that they are criminal enterprises. Some of them are pretty dopey and some of
them are very cunning, but at the end of the day what underpins the gangs is a criminal
enterprise. So what that needs is genuine, serious measures to address those problems,
not flimflam fluffery like this, and not puffery that looks like it does something but does
nothing. We need real measures. It starts w ith the people. It star ts with the social
problems and the economic problems, deals with the bad conduct, and provides real
measures to deal with bad conduct—the standover tactics, the intimidation, the theft, the
violence, the burglaries, and all the rest of it. It actually takes real measures, the sort of
stuff that the Hon Phil Goff introduced when he was a Minister of Justice. The one thing
that Phil Goff did not do was he did not le ave it up to members’ bills to look like and
give the appearance of doing something seri ous about a serious social problem. He took
the responsibility himself because he was a good Minister. We have not had a good
Minister of Justice for at least the last 5 year s, and that is part of the problem. We have
members—backbenchers—having to parade through this House, looking as if they are
doing something serious. Well, that is not happening. If we want to get real about
organised crime and get real about gangs, we need real legislatio n that is going to
address the real problems.
David Clendon from the Green Party was ri ght—and I was at the Justice Coalition
launch this afternoon—it is time to  get smart about crime. It is time to get smart about
crime, and when it comes to the ga ngs, it is about unders tanding the gangs,
understanding what drives them, dealing with  those issues, understa nding the antisocial
conduct they engage in, ad dressing the antisocial co nduct, and working with
communities to make them safer, as the Mu rupara Area School has shown it can do, the
principal of which tonight said that he was very concerned about this legislation because
he did not think it would wo rk. We need to actually take  real steps, not the half
measures that are represented by this bill.

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER-BELL
items.text: I rise to unequivocally  support the Prohibition
of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill, which is in the name of my colleague
Mark Mitchell, the member of Parliament fo r Rodney. I want to pay tribute to the work
that Mark has put into shepherding this bi ll through the House. It has been interesting
for me, as a new member, to see how he has applied his previous experience as a police
officer to inform the very constructive cont ribution that he has made during the debates
on this bill.
I should also acknowledge Mike Sabin, the me mber for Northland. It is so great to
see members using their practical, real-world experience in law enforcement in
supporting our communities at the front line, which is something that perhaps members
on the other side might know a little bit less about. Those National members are using
their practical experience to improve the law, which deals with some of the most
destructive, unpleasant, and violent entities in New Zealand.
I would also like to take this opportunity to acknow ledge the Hon Todd McClay,
who originally introduced this  member’s bill to the Hous e, and whose stewardship of
this legislation was interrupted only by his elevation to the executive.
12486 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 7 Aug 2013
I am delighted to support this bill, because it puts the rights of the majority of law-
abiding, respectful, and good citizens of our beautiful country ahead of those of the tiny,
hard-core, criminal minority who terrori se with both their offending and their
reputation. It is the reputation, in particular , of these gangs that this bill seeks to
neutralise. This bill strikes the right balan ce, in my view, between protecting the public
in a practicable way while not going so far as to create unintended consequences or
counter-productive situations. Fo r instance, gang patches—th at is, the signs, symbols,
and representations used to commonly denote membership or affiliation with a criminal
gang—will not be allowed on the premises  or grounds of our Public Service
departments, courthouses, police stations, loca l authority offices, and schools. But there
is a specific exclusion for Housing New Z ealand residential dwellings. The line has
been drawn, in my view, in a very sensible place, and we will not see families ejected
from their State homes because of admittedly ill-advised associations with gangs.
Similarly, tattoos or non-removable insigni a are not included as  grounds for banning
under this bill, so those with permanent ma rks of gang affiliations—perhaps as a result
of stupid decisions made in their youth—although they may be stigmatised by society,
are not going to be anathematised for life from setting foot on Government premises.
One has to hope that they take  the opportunity that this exce ption provides for to visit a
public hospital—the very fine public hospitals  we have in this country—and have their
gang tattoos removed by laser treatment so that they can rejoin decent society.
I want to focus on one particular element of the bill, and that is the ban on gang
insignia in schools and preschools. I support a ban on gang insignia in all governmental
premises in general, but I especially endorse the banning of gang insignia in schools and
educational institutions. I single these places ou t because it is crucial that the rangatahi,
the young people, who represent the future of  our country are protected as much as
possible from falling under the dark thrall of  the gangs. In those areas where gangs are
present, it is crucia l that we take a strong and determ ined approach to crack down on
gang culture and all that it re presents—the lawlessness, the violence, the disrespect of
other people, the ill-treatment of women a nd children, the trade in narcotics, and the
people-trafficking, not even to  mention the more petty but still harmful activities that
gangs perpetrate—and prevent these ills from being visited upon the next generation of
young Kiwis.
Unlike the other parties, with the excep tion of those who are supporting this bill—
and I acknowledge the member Richard Prosser for his passi onate speech in favour of
this legislation—I believe that if, through th is bill, one single person is diverted, one
single child is taken away from a wasted life of crime in the malevolent criminal
underbelly of this country, th en that would make this m easure worthwhile. I actually
believe that many, many kids will benefit from  this bill indirectly thanks to the clear
message that it sends, rejecting the culture of organised criminality. Schools around this
country, particularly in the most affected areas, agree with this.
As other members have done before me in th is debate, I would li ke to draw a small
quote from the submission to the Law and Order Committee by the chairman of the
board of trustees of Murupara Area School. Ja cob Te Kurapa JP, the chair, said that
“Murupara Area School is in support of this Bill for the following reasons: 1. Children
and students do not need to see gang insignia plastered about our school they need to be
protected from it.” He also said: “The intr oduction of gang insignia into our premises
would create tensions and unnecessary negativ e behaviour and we want to discourage
that type of behaviour from our  school. We have our own form  of ‘insignia’ and that is
the wearing of our uniform, so mething for our children to be proud of.” I am sure most
members in this House would agree with those sentiments.
7 Aug 2013 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 12487
I was quite surprised when Kris Faafoi ma de reference in his previous speech to
hearing that submission. He expressed his concern and his sympathy, but I think that the
people of this country, the children of Murupara Area School, and all concerned citizens
deserve more than concern. They deserve more than fine words. They deserve firm
action. That is why I am proud to be part of a Government that is delivering it, and
proud that I have a colleague like Mark Mitchell, who is actually giving the people of
New Zealand the action that they deserve an d that they need. So I have absolute
pleasure in commending this bill to the House.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I understand that the next call is a
split call.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere): I rise to take a short call on the
Government’s Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill. There are
some of us in this House who know a thi ng or two about gangs, having worked before
coming to this House in our community’s efforts to try to stop gang activity from
happening in the community or in our effort s with the community to try to stop our
young people from getting involved in gang-related activities, whether they be
legitimate or not, but primarily they have b een about drugs, violence , theft, and, in the
main, criminal activities. We on this side of the House, as I am sure is the same for
many others throughout this House, have no patience at all for gangs. I oppose gangs,
and Labour opposes gangs, and Labour opposes this particular bill. I will go through the
reasons why.
Despite what my colleague Kris Faafoi has said about the sincerity of Mark Mitchell
in bringing this bill forward, the reality is, when you really get down to it, this bill really
addresses the gang’s dress code. It does not address criminal activities perpetrated by
gangs. It does not address the drug dealings  that gangs get up to or the use of young
people to sell drugs. It does not address the thefts, the crim es, the violence, the beatings
that they give, or even, in some cases, rape  and murder. This bill does not address any
of those serious issues whatsoever. So Labour  is saying to this Government and to the
New Zealand public that this bill is a waste of time.
Regrettably, what this bill does and what the community is expecting this
Government to do are two different things. Yes, this Government has talked tough about
criminals. Yes, it has talked about how it was going to get tough with gangs, but the
reality is that this addresses only what gangsters should wear in a Government
department. It does not take away or address the substance or the character of the
gangster who is wearing the patch, and doe s not address the in timidation that the
gangster will impose on members of our public.
I do not know whether the member who has now taken up this bill is aware of the
changing environment with the gangsters. Most gangsters—most gangsters—no longer
wear patches. Yes, you would see motorcycle clubs wearing patches, but most gangsters
do not. Most gangsters are either doing their dealings deep underground, or particularly
out in the open wearing T-shirts. This is why I have made the point that this law does
not address the substantial issue that th e community is concerned about—criminal
activities by gangsters. It does not address that. So it is a waste of time.
Look, in 2010 the Otago University did a study  of the cost of legislation and found
that on average an Act costs around $3.5 million and a regulation costs around
$530,000. That is how much money that this Government is spending on a piece of
legislation that, effectively, wi ll not address the issues that  this community demands of
this Government that it address.
In fact, talking about the li nks between what this Government is doing and the gang-
related activities, or the reason why some  of our young people continue to go into
gangs, there is a clear link by the evidence that when there is unemployment, when
12488 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 7 Aug 2013
there is poverty—and the kinds of unemploym ent that we have seen recently in the
household labour force survey of 16.3 pe rcent unemployment for Pacific and 12.8
percent for M āori—that is the kind of thing that this Government is doing that is
perpetuating the kinds of activities that we see. So instead of the Government
addressing the hard issues of putting people into jobs and paying them decent wages, it
just prefers to deal with a dress code—a dress code—which does not address any of the
problems that I have outlined, which our communities throughout New Zealand are
concerned about. Criminal activities—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I rise as the Green Party s pokesperson on human rights to
speak to the third reading of this Prohibiti on of Gang Insignia on Government Premises
Bill. The Green Party opposes this bill. It  has been designed to feed the existing
widespread fear of gangs, without any chan ce of reducing the crime associated with
these gangs. This bill says that it seeks to restrict the display of gang insignia “on the
premises of Departments of the Public Servi ce, Statutory entities, and Local authorities
in New Zealand.”, and it define s “gangs” as “gangs listed within regulation”. The bill
will allow police to without warrant arrest  a person who the officer has good cause to
suspect has displayed a gang insignia on G overnment premises, and seize and remove
gang insignia that has been or is being disp layed. It also enables the police to stop
vehicles to exercise powers of arrest or seizure.
We have heard so much vitriol from th e Government side of the House about
criminality and the evil of gangs, yet none of us here is suggesting that gangs are
actually benign associations that contribute to our society. I join my Labour colleague in
sharing my experiences of working in the community and working in women’s refuges
with women who have escaped violence associated with gangs and have had to move
cities to be able to find freedom outside of  that environment. I have worked in youth
health, and I have seen young people being re cruited by the gangs. I have seen their
vulnerability and the danger that the gangs pr esent to them, but it is for these reasons
and based on these experiences that I oppose this bill and the Green Party opposes this
bill, and I would like to share some of the reasons why.
I am thinking particularly of those young people whom I have worked with. In the
recruiting of young people, gang patches are not part of the process; colours are. This
bill cannot do anything about that, and if it sought to actually make the wearing of
colours illegal, we would see how truly ridiculous this is.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Colours aren’t a patch.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: Colours are not a patch—exactly. But they serve the same purpose in
the recruitment of young people and the association of that gang. We would see, if we
outlawed the wearing of red T-shirts, how absolutely ludicrous this is.
Secondly, for me as a youth worker it was re ally important to be able to see that,
because it showed me those young people who were  at risk. It enabled me to have those
conversations with them and also for us to be able to go to the gangs at the time when
we saw patterns develop, and actually call them  on the safety of those young people. If
we drive this underground, if we hide this, th en we actually limit our ability to be able
to work with those young people to help them  actually find safe pathways to their own
futures. Thirdly, the gangs thrive on their ou tsider status. The more we take away and
demonise the regalia associated with the gangs , then the more we bui ld their status as
outsiders and the more alluring they become to those who have  been ostracised, or feel
they have been ostracised, by society. Fourth ly, we do not need this legislation. We
have the Summary Offences Ac t. We have numerous exampl es of police stations and
schools being able to say: “No gang patches on this site.” There is no need for it. There
7 Aug 2013 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 12489
is an ability to decide, as a community, ab out whether the visibility of patches is
appropriate in a specific place.
The Green Party is not pro-gang, but we ar e pro - solutions that work—not solutions
that demonise people but solutions that work  with people and communities. This is not
one of them.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: That speech from Jan Logie ensured that
the Green Party poll next time around will be well under 10 percent. The Green Party
says that it does not support this Prohibiti on of Gang Insignia in Government Premises
Bill but it does supports getting smart on crim e. What does that ac tually mean? What
that actually means is the Greens co-leade r Metiria Turei getti ng on television and
encouraging families to grow cannabis, advocating the growing of cannabis as a
legitimate and OK thing to do. That is what they think getting smart on crime is.
I want to just touch a little bit on those who have brought this bill to the House, Todd
McClay initially, before becoming a Mini ster, and Mark Mitchell. I want to
acknowledge the contribution of both of those members. I also want to acknowledge the
contribution of the New Zealand Police to maki ng New Zealand the safe society that on
the whole it is. The police are a bunch of men and women who do a very, very good job
for this nation. You do not have to go too far in the world to see that they are a fine
body of men and women serving the interests of this country well, and I want to
acknowledge them.
Ninety percent of organised crime in Ne w Zealand is gang re lated—90 percent of
organised crime. Gangs exist for a few reasons , but the core of them is to facilitate
criminal activity. At the top of the list is drug dealing, and right underneath that sit
prostitution, money-laundering, and standovers and intimidation. Often they all roll into
one. That is what gangs are th ere for. They are not clubs. They are not groups of people
who are doing any benefit to society whatso ever; they are outlaws. Everything that
Parliament can do to diminish their power to  do what they do to society is a positive
thing.
The gang patch and what it means is more significant to them than anything else.
Sometimes it is more significant to them than life itself. To earn a patch, gang members
will have to inflict on society the most heinous of crimes—robbery, grievous bodily
harm, and rape, to name but a few. But if a gang member wants to get an instant patch,
then it will be a homicide, and many have committed homicide simply to get that patch.
To them there is some badge-of-honour element to it. There is some badge-of-honour
element to it because to them it means everythi ng, and trying to take it off them is not a
case of just having a sign up.
The member Kris Faafoi—ironically his c onstituency of Mana includes Porirua,
where the police recruits are trained—tells us  the Porirua Police St ation has got a sign
saying “No gangs”, so that is OK, and we do not actually need this bill. Courts have
those signs as well. But what do police sta tions and courts gene rally have? That is
right—lots of people involved in enforcement and secur ity. What do school-grounds,
pools, parks, and the like have ? None of that. This bill  will give the police the
opportunity to get there and to lock those gang members up. If we followed Mr Faafoi’s
logic—although I am not sure that logic and Mr Faafoi ar e two things that would go
happily in one sentence—then all we would need to do is have signs around the place
about not committing crime: “No robberies he re”, “No rapes here”, and “No murders
here”, and that would take care of it because signs are going to take care of all criminal
activity.
He went on to say that what we really  should be doing is focusing on stopping youth
getting into gangs. I absolutely agree. My question to that member and to those on the

items.speaker: Opposition benches is
items.text: why do they vote agains t every initiative that we are putting in
12490 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 7 Aug 2013
place to give those young people a chance to get into work? Putting aside what we are
doing with the economy, why do they vote agai nst the welfare reforms that support 16
and 17-year-olds having the chance to have  the skills and the wr aparound support that
they need to get them work-ready? Why do they vote against the youth starting out
wage, which will give young Ne w Zealanders an opportunity to be employed and help
break down the barrier that young people ofte n face? Why do they vote against the 90-
day trial?
Those members vote against every effort. They will stand over there with their
disingenuous chanting and ranting about this  Government needing to do this and
needing to do that, but they will vote against us when we do try to do it. I am saying that
members cannot have it both ways. They seem to think they can, but the New Zealand
public have woken up to that. They are just wa ndering around in a sort  of yesteryear of
how the Labour Party used to operate, and they do not get that New Zealanders have
woken up to that.
The member the Hon Phil Goff, who has some  considerable experience in this area
and, certainly, in Parliament, says that this will be an offence at a school pool but it will
not be an offence down at the rugby league ground, and that it will be an offence under
the bus shelter but it will not be on the footpath beside it. Well, here is a bit of news for
Mr Goff. If he wants to read through the Summary Offences Act and the Crimes Act, he
will find that there are actually many offences that have location as a specific
ingredient, OK? This is not unique legislation. I do not see him wanting to repeal all
legislation that says something is an offence in a public place but not in a private place.

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: That wasn’t his point. The point was that it’s unworkable.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Well, the point is that Mr Goff  does not have a point—he does not
have a point. Mr Goff has to oppose, because Labour members have painted themselves
into a position where all they know is to  oppose. If you ask any New Zealander: “Who
on earth would oppose this?”—other than the Greens, because we expect that because
the Greens are sort of pro - criminal righ ts, and forget about the victims that the
criminals create—there is no on e. There is no one. Well, at least the La bour Party can
be guaranteed a few votes in  the 2014 election, from a few gang members—not that
they tend to vote very much, but it might pick up one or two out of that.
Mr Goff also went on about the drivers of crime, saying we must address the drivers
of crime. Well, that member’s party had 9 years to do something about the drivers of
crime that have fed gang culture and have ensured that gangs have exploded on to the
New Zealand scene in recent years. One was methamphetamine. They sat back there
and did nothing, saying “Oh, no, this problem is  all under control. Nothing to see here.
It will all go away.”
What has this Government done? There are just a few things—just a few headliners.
There is the Methamphetamine Action Pla n, banning precursors. The Government has
ramped up border controls and strategies ar ound dealing with intern ational transition of
precursors and drugs. It has changed search and surveillance laws significantly. It has
refocused the police to a focus on prevention and drivers of crime. It has changed bail
laws and put the onus on serious criminals to prove that people will  be safe. It has got
tougher sentencing laws for the most serious crimes. It has introduced drug courts. It
has doubled the amount of treatment in prisons—actually, we could go on and on.
The reality is that Labour Party members will stand up and say “Oh, they’ve got to
do something about this.”, but there is a reas on that crime is dropping. There is a reason
that crime is dropping. It is not some sort of gl obal trend that is occurring. It is actually
about smart, prudent policy, and about a Government that commits and does.
Opposition members have been decidedly de fensive about this, saying “Oh, we don’t
want to be getting soft on crime.” Well, what else can it be?
7 Aug 2013 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 12491
The thing that I find most ast ounding is that here is the Labour Party and—well, as I
say, we expect that from the Green Party; that is the watermelon patch way. When we
look at the Labour Party, it is opposing th e Government Communications Security
Bureau and Related Legislation Bill. We are actually fixing up what was actually a
loophole left just quietly on th e side there by Helen Clark some years ago. We are
actually fixing that up and putting tighter sc rutiny and controls around this. But no one
in the Labour Party would say we need this  legislation; they say we need a review.
Well, it is not about a review. They oppos e the Government Communications Security
Bureau legislation, which is designed to pr otect us from international terrorism and
those in New Zealand who are active in that, and they also oppose legislation about
domestic terrorism. That is what gangs reap on society.
I think that is a fairly sad indictment that  the Labour Party has got  right out of touch
with New Zealand, because they are opposing those two pieces of legislation that are
very deep in the hearts of New Zealanders. What is the Labour Party actually standing
up for? It is not standing up for New Zealanders. And will this bill make a difference?
Well, damn right it will make a difference. As a former police officer I know how much
it will make a difference to be able to ta ke that patch off that gang member, and how
much it will make a difference to be able to reduce the intimidation that gang members
inflict on us. They are nothing more than a parasitical blight on New Zealand society.
They are a cancer, and they feed off their hos t, and their host is the children of New
Zealand citizens.
Who else, other than the Labour Party and the Green Party, would actually think that
voting against this was a good idea? Well, they are all listed in the bill. There is a whole
range of gangs. No one other than those peop le would vote against this. To me it is a
sad indictment and a demonstration that they are out of touch. This is a good bill.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Spit it out.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: In a minute. This is a good bill. It  will be effective law. The public
want it. The police want it. The gangs do not, and the message from this Government to
the gang members is: “Gang members, no more patchies for you.”
